title: 'It Took 10 Days to Convince Me': Ganguly Reveals Why Dhoni's India Call-Up Was Delayed
excerpt: The former captain's admission sheds new light on the most consequential selection gamble in Indian cricket history
body:
Sourav Ganguly has built a reputation for candour in retirement, but his latest revelation about MS Dhoni's path to the Indian team is among his most striking. In a recent interview, the former captain admitted that he deliberately delayed Dhoni's call-up to the national side, choosing to first assess the young wicketkeeper-batsman's domestic performances in Jamshedpur before committing to what would become Indian cricket's most transformative selection.

"It took 10 days to convince me," Ganguly said, describing the behind-the-scenes deliberations that preceded Dhoni's eventual inclusion in the 2004 squad. The delay, far from being a bureaucratic oversight, was a conscious decision by a captain who wanted to see whether the raw power he had heard about could translate to higher levels.

## The Jamshedpur scouting mission

Ganguly's hands-on approach to talent identification was unusual for an Indian captain. Rather than relying solely on selector recommendations, he tracked Dhoni's domestic performances personally, particularly in Jharkhand's Ranji Trophy campaigns. Former India coach John Wright later confirmed that Ganguly had been keen to include Dhoni in the squad for India's 2004 tour of Pakistan — a high-stakes assignment that ultimately went to Parthiv Patel instead.

The decision to hold Dhoni back was not about doubt in his ability. Ganguly has consistently spoken about recognising Dhoni's six-hitting power from the earliest scouting reports. The delay was about readiness — ensuring that a player from outside India's traditional cricket infrastructure could handle the pressure of international competition.

"I liked his Phase 1," Ganguly recalled, referring to Dhoni's explosive early batting style. "He was a chabuk new batsman — he could change the game in an over."

## From Ranchi to the world

Dhoni's backstory is well known but no less remarkable for its familiarity. A ticket collector at Kharagpur railway station, he left a stable Indian Railways job to pursue cricket full-time — a decision that horrified his family. His breakthrough came in the 2004 Duleep Trophy final, where a 60-run innings sealed his place in the national reckoning.

His ODI debut against Bangladesh in December 2004, at 23 years and 169 days, was unremarkable — a duck. But his fifth ODI, a century at Vizag against Pakistan, announced a talent that would go on to win India three ICC trophies and redefine wicketkeeper-batting worldwide.

The 10-day delay that Ganguly describes is, in hindsight, a footnote. But it illuminates something essential about Indian cricket's selection machinery in the early 2000s: that even the most gifted players needed a champion within the system. Dhoni found his in Ganguly.

## Why the diaspora cares

For NRI cricket fans, Dhoni is more than a cricketer. He is a cultural touchstone — the small-town outsider who conquered Indian cricket without the establishment pedigree of a Tendulkar or a Dravid. His journey from Ranchi to the World Cup final resonates deeply with diaspora communities who understand what it means to succeed outside conventional pathways.

Ganguly's revelation adds texture to a story that the diaspora has claimed as its own. The idea that even Dhoni — who would go on to become India's most successful captain — needed someone to fight for his place is both humbling and instructive. In cricket, as in the immigrant experience, talent alone is never quite enough.

## The legacy question

Ganguly's admission also reopens a question about his own legacy. His tenure as India captain is remembered for aggressive cricket and blooding young talent — Harbhajan Singh, Yuvraj Singh, Zaheer Khan, and Dhoni among them. But the 10-day hesitation suggests that even Ganguly, for all his instinct, wrestled with the uncertainty that accompanies every selection gamble.

That he got Dhoni right — eventually — is the kind of captain's call that defines careers. Not Ganguly's career, which was already assured, but Dhoni's, and through Dhoni's, the trajectory of Indian cricket itself.
